extra.message: Authorization check relies on a client-controlled cookie ("ops_badge") or header ("x-ops-badge"). Setting this value to "lead" grants elevated privileges. This is trivially bypassed by any client.

The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is set to the value of the request Origin header (mirrored), combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This allows any website to make credentialed cross-origin requests, enabling CSRF-like attacks from malicious origins.

extra.message: SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled via ssl._create_unverified_context(). This allows man-in-the-middle attacks against outbound HTTPS connections, enabling interception of sensitive data.

random.choice() is used to generate a security-sensitive nonce/code instead of secrets.choice(). random is not cryptographically secure and its output is predictable, allowing attackers to guess generated codes.

extra.message: The X-XSS-Protection header is explicitly set to "0" (disabling browser XSS filter) and Content-Security-Policy is set to empty string (disabling CSP). This removes browser-side security protections against XSS attacks.

SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded fallback value "unsafe-local-dev-secret-key-change-me" when DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. If deployed to production without the environment variable, this weak default would compromise session signing, CSRF tokens, and other cryptographic operations.

django.shortcuts.redirect() is called with notification.url, which is a user-populated CharField stored in the database. If an attacker can inject a notification record with an external URL, users clicking the notification will be redirected off-site. Django's redirect() will follow any URL string.
